forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
intro: Twelve bars are enough for this brisk D major bourrée: a short strain, a longer answer, and both repeated. Michelle Rakers and the Marine Chamber Orchestra play the whole dance three times.

sections.label: A · The twelve-bar dance
sections.mNote: Four bars answered by eight, each strain repeated

sections.label: A · The dance again
sections.mNote: The upbeat starts a second round of both strains

sections.label: A′ · The final round
sections.mNote: The same two strains lead to the last D major chord

cues.title: An upbeat and twelve bars
cues.text: One upbeat launches the dance. A four-bar phrase is repeated, then an eight-bar answer is repeated too. The tune moves in quick, even notes, with the bass keeping its own steady stride underneath.
cues.evidence: Samuel Arnold’s full score, The Celebrated Water-musick (1788), pp. 49–50: upbeat, four-bar and eight-bar strains with repeat signs. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(26_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A catch before the cadence
cues.text: The dance makes its third circuit. At the end of the longer strain, a note hangs over the bass before dropping a step: the little 4–3 suspension written beneath the stave. Then the chord settles on D major.
cues.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), p. 50: 4–3 figures before the final D major chord, bars 11–12. The established section marks the third complete pass. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_celebrated_Water-musick._In_score._Composed_in_the_year_1716._By_G._F._Handel_-_btv1b10072587v_(27_of_30).jpg
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: D major, then the upbeat again
transitions.how: A 4–3 suspension delays the last cadence of the eight-bar strain. The bass reaches D and the upper parts hold the D major chord. The upbeat then starts the dance again, with no linking passage between the two rounds.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 49–50: the closing suspension and D major chord, then the opening upbeat. The existing sections identify the three complete passes.

transitions.title: One more round of the dance
transitions.how: The second round closes on the same D major chord. The upbeat immediately recalls the opening, and the short and long strains make their last circuit. Both retain their repeats and the bass returns to D at the final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Arnold’s full score (1788), pp. 49–50: the two repeated strains and their closing cadence. The established section boundary marks the third pass.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The wide shot in this video’s thumbnail shows a harpsichord at stage left, strings with a double bass and a bassoon; a trumpet is visible in the Hornpipe video, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each of the three passes is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 0:34, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (15 of the three suites) and the structure heard (a four-bar and an eight-bar strain, each repeated, the whole air played three times) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text and its instruction “This Air to be played 3 times over”; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured pauses and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 12 bars with repeat signs and the instruction on p. 53; IMSLP lists the movement as 12 bars played three times (36). The higher level of the third pass is a feature of this performance: the printed notes are the same for all three.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. The Handel group stands after the intermission in the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

fields.note: This is a U.S.-jurisdiction statement, not a claim of worldwide status. The programme carries a general notice that a performance may contain third-party material and should not be assumed to be public domain; no third-party material is identified in this performance of a composition from before 1759, but the notice is recorded here. The official Marine Band YouTube channel published the source video.

composer.epithet: He filled London theatres with Italian opera, then put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg offered something noisier: a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant; Prince Ruspoli gave him singers and instrumentalists to write for. The Dixit Dominus of 1707 sends five choral parts racing through a Latin psalm, then makes them hold dissonant notes while the other voices move underneath. His chamber cantatas tried the same arts of persuasion with a single singer. Corelli’s Rome taught him what a violin could say beside a voice.
